text: of influenza vaccine is about 70 to 90%, and vaccination of the elderly living in the community reduces the number of hospitalisations by 25 to 39% and death by 39 to 75%.8 No vaccine is currently available for avian in- fluenza.2,11 Four antiviral drugs are available for the prevention of in- fluenza: the M2 ion channel inhibitors, amantadine and rimantadine, and the neuraminidase inhibitors, oseltamivir and zanamivir. Antivirals appear to act independently of vaccination and provide additional barriers to the virus, but should not be used as a substitute for vaccination. They may be considered for postexposure prophylaxis, for sea- sonal prophylaxis in unvaccinated individuals at high risk, for persons who take care of those at high risk, and in vac- cinated individuals if an influenza outbreak occurs less than 2 weeks after vaccination with an inactivated vaccine, or if circulating influenza strains are thought to be different to the vaccine strain. Prophylaxis with antivirals may also be considered in vaccinated immunocompromised indi- viduals whose antibody response to the vaccine is likely to be incomplete.11,12 Amantadine and rimantadine, when started before expo- sure and continued throughout the period of exposure, are effective in preventing influenza A in 60 to 90% of pa- tients. They are ineffective against influenza B and there- fore cannot be considered as a substitute for vaccination unless the vaccine is contra-indicated.11,13 Additional problems with these drugs are the rapid development of viral resistance and subsequent spread of resistant virus to close contacts and the potential to cause serious CNS ad- verse effects. Clinical studies in healthy adults indicate that both the neu- raminidase inhibitors, oseltamivir and zanamivir are effec- tive in preventing infection with influenza A and B in about 80% of individuals and both have been reported to prevent illness in persons in close contact with infected household members.14,15 In the USA, all 4 antiviral drugs are licensed for prophy- laxis of influenza but only oseltamivir and zanamivir are recommended by the Advisory Committee on Immuniza- tion Practices10 and the American Academy of Pediat- rics.16 In the UK, amantadine and oseltamivir are licensed for prophylaxis, but only oseltamivir is recommended by 860 Antivirals NICE17 for postexposure prophylaxis in persons 13 years of age or older at high risk of complications of influenza. Neither drug is recommended for seasonal prophylaxis of influenza. For most people treatment of influenza is largely sympto- matic and supportive. However, antivirals may be used for the treatment of vaccinated or unvaccinated individuals who develop symptoms. Amantadine and rimantadine have been shown to reduce the duration of uncomplicated influenza A infection when given within 48 hours of the onset of symptoms.
